title: Evaluating Pathways Involved in Melanoma Initiation
text:
PROJECT DESCRIPTION
Cancer initiates from zones of cells that are preprogrammed to transition to malignant cell states. We plan to
examine signaling pathways that activate cancer from these cancer precursor zones (CPZ) and have identified
ApoD as a gene that causes the transition from a CPZ to a tumor by conferring resistance to oxidative stress.
We plan to examine initiating clones of melanoma. Our studies will have an impact on understanding how cancer
starts and may allow for the development of more accurate diagnoses and treatments that could prevent cancer.

title: Aging and HIV Scientific Working Group
text: PROJECT SUMMARY—AGING AND HIV SCIENTIFIC WORKING GROUP As the population of people with HIV (PWH) continues to age, the intersection of HIV and aging presents an urgent and underexplored area of biomedical research. Older PWH face disproportionately high rates of frailty, neurocognitive impairment, cardiovascular disease, and non-AIDS-defining cancers, driven by both HIV-related factors and accelerated biological aging. Compounding these challenges are critical psychosocial issues, including stigma, isolation, and disparities in care, including among those with perinatally acquired HIV. Despite these growing needs, there is limited infrastructure for interdisciplinary research, training, and translation in HIV and aging. To address this gap, the Aging and HIV Scientific Working Group (SWG) will serve as a regional and national working group embedded within the Texas Center for AIDS Research (CFAR), uniting leading institutions across Texas with expertise in virology, geroscience, immunology, behavioral health, and community engagement. Leveraging strong collaborations with the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston’s Institute on Aging, Baylor College of Medicine’s Huffington Center on Aging, the Gulf Coast Consortium on Aging and Geroscience, and the researchers and infrastructure at Texas Biomedical Research Institute, the SWG will catalyze research that integrates mechanistic and translational approaches across model systems and human cohorts. The SWG will pursue three interlocking aims: 1) expand interdisciplinary collaborations through annual Aging-HIV symposia, embedded content in regional and national meetings, and new cross-disciplinary research teams; 2) support early-stage and team-based research via targeted pilot grants, with a focus on NIH grant conversion and integration of CFAR core resources; and 3) build a sustained research community through a dedicated working group supporting quarterly convenings, community involvement, and translational project development. Structured mentorship, training workshops, and grant development pipelines will foster career advancement for new investigators. Through these efforts, the Aging and HIV SWG will bridge basic and clinical research, extend geroscience principles into HIV studies, and foster culturally informed approaches to HIV-aging interventions. Impact will be measured through interdisciplinary collaborations, pilot-to-R grant conversions, scientific outputs, and the engagement of populations in research. It will function as a dynamic interface between the biological and social dimensions of aging with HIV and will align with national HIV-aging priorities. By institutionalizing collaborative research, training, and community engagement at this intersection, the Aging and HIV SWG will position the Texas CFAR as a national leader in addressing one of the most pressing challenges in contemporary HIV science.

title: Molecular mechanisms of anterior segment disorders
text:
Anterior segment disorders represent a significant cause of blindness and vision loss. Current understanding of
the genetic causes of these conditions is incomplete. This project will utilize human samples, modern computer
analyses, and in vitro and in vivo studies, including the pioneering application of the ‘eye development in a dish’
and the zebrafish model to uncover novel causes of these debilitating eye phenotypes.

title: ECHO Laboratory Core at Vanderbilt for Integrated Sample Biobanking and Processing
text:
The NIH has established the Environmental influences on Child Health Outcomes (ECHO) Program, a
collaborative multi-dimensional research initiative to characterize the impact of early-life environmental factors
(e.g., social-environmental, parental risk factors, nicotine, diet, infection) on childhood health. Vanderbilt will
support ECHO by establishing the ECHO Laboratory Core at Vanderbilt for Integrated Sample Tracking and
Processing (ELVIS), to facilitate the collection and processing of biospecimens; manage the biorepository;
performs a wide range of biospecimen assays (including novel development), and coordinate metadata and
assay data transfer to the Coordinating Center. Successful completion will enable the success of ECHO’s
mission to discover molecular underpinnings of early childhood determinants of disease.

title: Defining Drivers of HPV-associated Carcinogenesis
text:
Human papillomaviruses (HPV) cause 5% of human cancers. While there are highly effective, prophylactic HPV
vaccines, their poor uptake in the US combined with the fact that they do not treat existing persistent
infections or the cancers arising from those pre-existing infections necessitates that we continue efforts to
learn how to eliminate persistent HPV infections and the cancers they cause. These are the goals of this grant.
Project Narrative

title: mHealth Technologies for Assessing Blood Perfusion in Chronic Wounds
text:
There is an unmet need for a low-cost system that can access tissue perfusion during chronic wound care
during telehealth consultations. We will implement and validate a smartphone-based system to characterize
functional and structural information about the wound, such as vascular structure and hemoglobin in the vessel’s
bloodstream. The technology can lead to faster and more precise measurement of wound healing to optimize
medication and therapy interventions.

title: Macropinocytosis and Pulmonary Fibrosis
text:
Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is the most common cause of pulmonary fibrosis worldwide. IPF is a chronic,
progressive, and lethal lung disease affecting approximately 200,000 patients in the US and more than 5 million
people worldwide with steadily increasing incidence and mortality.
This project will determine the key roles of
macropinocytosis and its mechanism(s) in the pathogenesis of pulmonary fibrosis, using a combination of in
vitro, in vivo and ex vivo experimental approaches.

title: Preclinical-Clinical Trials Collaboration to effectively advance new combination therapies for malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors
text:
The goal of this collaborative translational research project is to utilize insight into cell signaling, cancer biology,
immunology, mouse tumor models and developmental therapeutics to rationally develop and test new
combination therapies in patients with unresectable NF1 MPNSTs. This work will be performed as a partnership
between Karen Cichowski (extramural PI, basic science, preclinical studies), Brigitte Widemann (intramural PI,
clinical studies), AeRang Kim (extramural co-PI, clinical studies) and Jack Shern (intramural Co-PI basic science,
correlative studies on clinical trials) to enhance the translation of basic biological discoveries into clinical
applications for NF1 patients. Ultimately this effort will provide the foundation for an iterative enterprise, in that
insight and samples from the clinic will be used to help develop new therapeutic approaches.

title: Modulation of Oligodendrocyte Development by Voltage-Operated Calcium Channels
text:
The objective of this proposal is to determine the role of voltage-gated calcium channels
in oligodendrocyte development and myelination of the central nervous system. This work is
relevant to developing means to induce remyelination in myelin degenerative diseases and for
myelin repair in damaged nervous tissue.

title: Overcoming innate drug efflux systems to expand anthelmintic vulnerability
text:
The aim of the project is to investigate ATP-binding cassette transporters that remove
antiparasitic drugs from nematode cells. Inhibition of unique P-glycoproteins will enable
restoration of efficacy for multiple existing anthelmintic drugs. The project is relevant to the
NIH mission of protecting the public from eukaryotic infectious diseases, such as parasites.

title: Engineering Yeast towards High Titer Production of Monoterpene Indole Alkaloid Natural Products
text:
Plant natural products and plant natural product-derived drugs have been indispensible towards
the treatment of different diseases and the prophylactic maintenance of healthy lifestyle. In this
proposal, we aim to use synthetic biology strategies for yeast-based, high-titer production of
monoterpene indole alkaloids, a family of plant compounds of which many are therapeutically
important.

title: Therapeutic Potential of ALK1 Activating Drugs in HHT Models
text:
(NARRATIVE ATTACHMENT)
Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is a highly debilitating genetic bleeding disorder for which no
effective cure is currently available. In this application, we propose determining whether a newly identified
antibody targeting the ALK1 receptor could have disease-modifying properties in HHT experimental models. This
strategy could pave the way for new clinical investigations in HHT.

title: Binge Eating as a Mechanism Underlying the Food Insecurity-Obesity Paradox in Adolescents
text: Food insecurity is paradoxically associated with elevated risk of adolescent obesity in the United States. The mechanisms underlying this excess risk are not well understood, and such knowledge is essential for informing obesity prevention efforts for adolescents from under-resourced backgrounds. Thus, aligned with the need emphasized by the Strategic Plan for NIH Obesity Research to identify the reasons contributing to increased risk for obesity among economically marginalized populations, research is critically needed to elucidate modifiable mechanisms to target in obesity prevention efforts among food-insecure adolescents. In the proposed project, Dr. Hazzard, a registered dietitian and public health researcher, will examine binge eating as a potential mechanism to explain the association between food insecurity and elevated risk for adolescent obesity. The K99 phase of this Pathway to Independence Award supported Dr. Hazzard in filling critical training gaps and conducting the research necessary to launch her career as an independent investigator conducting intervention work to promote food security and healthy weight among adolescents experiencing food insecurity. Through coursework, mentorship, and research, Dr. Hazzard gained expertise in (1) qualitative and mixed methods, (2) advanced statistical methods, with a focus on machine learning and causal mediation analysis, and (3) intervention design, development, and dissemination, with an emphasis on human-centered design. During the mentored K99 phase, she worked to elucidate the etiology of binge eating in the context of food insecurity during adolescence using a mixed-methods approach that involved (a) conducting qualitative interviews in foodinsecure adolescents who report binge eating and (b) leveraging existing data from an NIH-funded observational cohort to employ tree-based machine learning techniques. In the independent R00 phase, Dr. Hazzard will recruit 175 adolescents into a new, independent cohort that she will follow for 18 months to quantify the extent to which binge eating mediates the longitudinal association between food insecurity and weight gain during adolescence (Aim 1 of the R00 phase). Finally, using a human-centered design approach, she will develop vignettes describing potential interventions in community settings to improve food security and prevent excess weight gain among food-insecure adolescents and assess perceived acceptability of the potential interventions using these vignettes in semi-structured interviews with adolescents who have experienced food insecurity (Aim 2 of the R00 phase). Findings from this project will lay the groundwork for the development and implementation of an intervention in a community setting to promote food security and healthy weight among adolescents experiencing food insecurity and, in turn, promote Dr. Hazzard’s successful transition to an independent research career.

title: Machine Learning and Automated Flow Synthesis for the Development of Peptide Catalysts for the Stereo- and Site-Selective Formation of C–C Bonds
text:
Expedient access to new treatments for human disease is predicated on synthetic methods that can
construct C–C bonds with pinpoint stereo- and site- selectivity. This proposal comprises a platform that fills in
the middle ground between biocatalysts and small molecule peptide catalysts for the rational development of
mid-length peptide catalysts. Utilizing an automated fast-flow peptide synthesizer and machine learning models,
we will rapidly generate peptide catalysts and rationally explore chemical space to achieve the desired reactivity
and selectivity.

title: Heterogeneity in joint real-time and developmental influences of positive and negative social media experiences on socioemotional vulnerability and psychopathology across adolescence
text:
PROJECT NARRATIVE.
Our understanding of social media as a key developmental context for adolescent mental health is currently
limited by a focus on average effects across individuals and time. Innovation is needed to move beyond
average effects to identify who is at risk (or can benefit), via what type of social media interpersonal
experiences, when in real-time or development, and by which pathway risk escalates or remits. In this project
we will, (1) chart real-time links in differential susceptibility to positive and negative online social experiences
across individuals, (2) test whether short term effects accumulate over time to amplify or buffer risk for
psychopathology, and (3) identify the relative developmental contributions of online vs. in-person
socioemotional experiences to growth in psychopathology risk across adolescence.

title: Under Pressure: Biophysical Mapping of Herpesvirus Capsid Assembly and Genome Packaging
text:
Herpesviruses infect most of the human population, establishing incurable, lifelong, dormant infections that upon
reactivation, can result in severe disease states and fatalities, particularly among the immunocompromised. The
complexity of these viruses, along with divergent aspects of viral replication among the three subfamilies infecting
humans, have hindered the identification of pan-herpesviral preventions and treatments. Therefore, the goal of
this proposal is to develop a deep understanding of how herpesvirus capsids assemble and package DNA, two
essential steps required for all herpesviruses to spread infection, and use this information to develop novel
therapeutic interventions.

title: Spatial control of membrane traffic by septin GTPases
text:
Defects in the internal organization of cells and the transport mechanisms of their proteins and
membranes underlie the pathogenesis of many human diseases including cancer,
neurodegeneration (e.g., Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, ALS), brain injury and metabolic disorders.
This research program aims to advance our knowledge of how transport within cells is spatially
controlled by a unique family of proteins called septins. The proposed research will advance basic
knowledge of cell biology, which in the long-term will be used to design better treatments that can
reverse or slow down disease and/or to regenerate ailing cells and tissues.

title: Assessing the Efficacy of Mindfulness Apps
text:
Mental health apps, specifically mindfulness apps, are popular tools
people increasingly turn to as preventive, first-line, or adjunctive care for depression. But the
current literature lacks rigorous, unbiased studies assessing the efficacy of these apps. This study
is designed to assess and address these critical issues by (a) employing a novel digital placebo
control condition, (b) matching people to a mindfulness app that may be the most effective for
their unique needs, and thus, accounting for personal preferences and the Digital Working
Alliance, and (c) implementing smartphone digital phenotyping to build personalized and
population level models of response that can be used to understand how symptoms, behavior,
and environment impact patients’ response to mindfulness apps.

title: Investigating the evolutionary and clinical implications of tumor suppressor allele dosage
text:
Acquired treatment resistance is a common but unpredictable problem relevant to a wide variety
of therapies and cancer types. Recently, I demonstrated that genomic information from a pre-
treatment breast cancer sample can not only predict worse outcomes to a common form of
breast cancer therapy but also forecast the precise mechanism of treatment resistance that is
likely to emerge. In this proposal, I will deploy advanced machine learning techniques and
multimodal sequencing technologies to refine this predictive ability, as well as to expand our
findings to a wide variety of genes, treatments, and cancer types.

title: Harnessing large biobanks to decipher cancer pleiotropy
text:
While studies to date have only identified a portion of the genetic risk factors underlying cancer risk, identifying
genetic regions that contribute to multiple cancers provides a unique opportunity to identify shared mechanisms
underlying cancer risk. In this study, we will harness existing rich genomic data and resources, including biobanks
with newly developed whole-genome sequencing, to conduct in-depth cancer studies at scale. Findings are
expected to close critical gaps in our understanding of shared cancer heritability, while identifying novel cancer
risk loci that will further our mechanistic insights into cancer development.
